record.content_text:
Suppose there are 4 cakes available for Oluchi's birthday party. The cakes are quite small, so she wants each person to have $\frac{2}{3}$ of a cake. How will Oluchi know how many people will get cake?

Oluchi must calculate $4\div\frac{2}{3}$. Because she wants each person to get two thirds, $\frac{2}{3}$, she must start by cutting each cake into 3 pieces.

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-030.png)

Now she must work out how many people can each get $\frac{2}{3}$ of a cake.

record_links.rationale: This worked example solves whole-number-by-fraction division using diagrams.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 6.10: Dividing using diagrams: whole number ÷ fraction

record.evidence_quote: Calculate: $$ 4\div\frac{2}{3} $$
record.prompt_text:
Calculate:

$$
4\div\frac{2}{3}
$$
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Represent all the parts of the whole number, according to the denominator of the fraction.

The denominator of the fraction is 3. We must divide 4 shapes into 3 parts each.

![diagram 1](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-030.png)

Step 2: Determine how many times the numerator of the fraction can be counted.

The numerator is 2. This means every 2 parts represents one count.

![diagram 2](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-031.png)

Step 3: Write down the answer.

There are 6 different colours. We can count every $\frac{2}{3}$ six times. This means at Oluchi's birthday party, 6 people can each get $\frac{2}{3}$ of a cake.

$$
4\div\frac{2}{3}=6
$$

heading_path.h3: Worked example 6.11: Using a reciprocal to divide: whole number ÷ fraction

record.evidence_quote: Calculate: $$ 4\div\frac{2}{3} $$
record.prompt_text:
Calculate:

$$
4\div\frac{2}{3}
$$
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Regard division as another form of multiplication.

Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by the reciprocal of the fraction.

$$
4\div\frac{2}{3}=4\times\frac{3}{2}
$$

Step 2: Follow the short method for multiplying whole numbers and fractions.

Denominator: $\frac{\phantom{00}}{2}$

Numerator: $4\times3=12$

Calculation:

$$
\begin{array}{l}
 \phantom{00}4\times\frac{3}{2}\\
 =\frac{4\times3}{2} \\
 =\frac{12}{2}\\
 =\;6
 \end{array}
$$

record.content_text:
At Ifetayo's birthday party, there is only $\frac{3}{4}$ of one cake left. Ifetayo wants to share this equally between her two best friends, so that they can take it home.

The cake that is left may be represented as follows:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-024.png)

Now Ifetayo must figure out how she is going to share this equally between her two friends.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 6.12: Dividing using a diagram: fraction ÷ whole number

record.evidence_quote: Calculate: $$ \frac{3}{4}\div2 $$
record.prompt_text:
Calculate:
$$
\frac{3}{4}\div2
$$
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Use a diagram to represent the fraction.

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-024.png)

Step 2: Divide the shape further, according to the whole number.
The whole number is 2. If we want to share the shaded portion between 2 people, we must divide each shaded part into 2 parts.

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-032.png)

Step 3: Share the shaded parts equally, according to the whole number.
The whole number is 2. If we want to share the shaded parts equally between 2 people, we simply allocate them to person 1 and person 2.

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-033.png)

Step 4: Write down the fraction that each person gets.
If we divide $\frac{3}{4}$ between two people, each person gets $\frac{3}{8}$.

Step 5: Write down the answer.
$$
\frac{3}{4}\div2=\frac{3}{8}
$$

heading_path.h3: Worked example 6.13: Using a reciprocal to divide: fraction ÷ whole number

record.evidence_quote: Calculate: $$ \frac{3}{4}\div2 $$
record.prompt_text:
Calculate:
$$
\frac{3}{4}\div2
$$
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Regard division as another form of multiplication.
Dividing by a whole number is the same as multiplying by the reciprocal of the whole number.

$$
\frac{3}{4}\times\frac{1}{2}
$$

Step 2: Follow the short method for multiplying fractions with fractions.
$$
\frac{3}{4}\times\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3\times1}{4\times2}=\frac{3}{8}
$$

record.content_text:
Remember that there was only $\frac{3}{4}$ of one cake left at Ifetayo's birthday party. Suppose, instead of dividing this between her two best friends, she rather decides to give $\frac{1}{8}$ of the cake to as many people as possible.

We already know the cake that is left may be represented as follows:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-024.png)

Now Ifetayo must figure out how many people can get $\frac{1}{8}$ of the cake to take home. She must calculate $\frac{3}{4}\div\frac{1}{8}$.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 6.14: Using a diagram to divide: fraction ÷ fraction

record.evidence_quote: Calculate: $$ \frac{3}{4}\div\frac{1}{8} $$
record.prompt_text:
Calculate:
$$
\frac{3}{4}\div\frac{1}{8}
$$
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Use a diagram to represent the first fraction.

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-024.png)

Step 2: Divide the shape further, until the parts are equal to the denominator of the second fraction.
The denominator of the second fraction is 8.

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-032.png)

Step 3: Determine how many times the numerator of the second fraction can be counted from the shaded parts.
The numerator of the second fraction is 1. This means every part represents one count. Remember that we can only count shaded parts.

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-034.png)

Step 4: Write down the answer.
There are six different colours. We can count every $\frac{1}{8}$ six times. This means that 6 people can each take home $\frac{1}{8}$ of the cake.

$$
\frac{3}{4}\div\frac{1}{8}=6
$$

record.evidence_quote: There are various methods that may be used to multiply and divide mixed numbers. It is recommended that you first convert all mixed numbers to improper fractions before you multiply or divide.

record_links.rationale: This worked example divides mixed numbers by converting to improper fractions and multiplying by the reciprocal.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 6.16: Dividing mixed numbers

record.evidence_quote: Calculate: $$2\frac{5}{8}\div3\frac{3}{4}$$
record.prompt_text:
Calculate:

$$2\frac{5}{8}\div3\frac{3}{4}$$
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions.

$$2\frac{5}{8}=\frac{(8\times2)+5}{8}=\frac{21}{8}$$

$$3\frac{3}{4}=\frac{(4\times3)+3}{4}=\frac{15}{4}$$

Step 2: Regard division as another form of multiplication.

Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by the reciprocal of the fraction.

$$\frac{21}{8}\times\frac{4}{15}$$

Step 3: Write down the first step for multiplying fractions by fractions. Then see whether there are numerator and denominator pairs that have common factors.

$$\frac{21\times4}{8\times15}$$

The HCF of 4 and 8 is 4.
The HCF of 21 and 15 is 3.

If necessary, go back to Chapter 2 to revise how to find the highest common factor (HCF) of two or more numbers.

$$\frac{\color{red}{4}\; \color{black}{\times}\; \color{green}{21}}{\color{red}{8}\; \color{black}{\times}\;\color{green}{15}}$$

Step 4: Divide by the common factors you identified in Step 3.

$$\frac{\color{red}{4\div4}\; \color{black}{\times}\; \color{green}{21\div3}}{\color{red}{8\div4}\; \color{black}{\times}\;\color{green}{15\div3}}$$

Step 5: Write down the simplified expression and calculate the answer.

$$\frac{1\times7}{2\times5}=\frac{7}{10}$$

Step 6: Check that the answer is in its simplest form. Write improper fractions as mixed numbers.

In this case, the answer is in its simplest form.

heading_path.h3: Exercise 6.9: Multiply and divide mixed numbers

record.evidence_quote: Source math retained: 7 rac{1}{8}= rac{(8 imes7)+1}{8}= rac{57}{8} 4 rac{3}{4}= rac{(4 imes4)+3}{4}= rac{19}{4} rac{57}{8}\div rac{19}{4}= rac{57}{8} \times \frac{4}{19}= \frac{57\times4}{8\times19} rac{(57\div19)\times(4\div4)}{(19\div19)\times(8\div4)}=\frac{3\times1}{1\times2}=\frac{3}{2}=1\frac{1}{2}
record.prompt_text:
### Exercise 6.9: Multiply and divide mixed numbers

3. $7\frac{1}{8}\div4\frac{3}{4}$
record.answer_text:
$$7\frac{1}{8}=\frac{(8\times7)+1}{8}=\frac{57}{8}$$
$$4\frac{3}{4}=\frac{(4\times4)+3}{4}=\frac{19}{4}$$
$$\frac{57}{8}\div\frac{19}{4}=\frac{57}{8} \times \frac{4}{19}= \frac{57\times4}{8\times19}$$
The HCF of 4 and 8 is 4.
The HCF of 57 and 19 is 19.
$$\frac{(57\div19)\times(4\div4)}{(19\div19)\times(8\div4)}=\frac{3\times1}{1\times2}=\frac{3}{2}=1\frac{1}{2}$$

record_links.rationale: This item asks learners to divide mixed numbers.

heading_path.h3: Exercise 6.9: Multiply and divide mixed numbers

record.evidence_quote: Source math retained: 4 rac{1}{6}= rac{(6 imes4)+1}{6}= rac{25}{6} 3 rac{8}{9}= rac{(9 imes3)+8}{9}= rac{35}{9} rac{25}{6}\div rac{35}{9}= rac{25}{6} \times \frac{9}{35}= \frac{25\times9}{6\times35} rac{(25\div5)\times(9\div3)}{(35\div5)\times(6\div3)}=\frac{5\times3}{7\times2}=\frac{15}{14}=1\frac{1}{14}
record.prompt_text:
### Exercise 6.9: Multiply and divide mixed numbers

4. $4\frac{1}{6}\div3\frac{8}{9}$
record.answer_text:
$$4\frac{1}{6}=\frac{(6\times4)+1}{6}=\frac{25}{6}$$
$$3\frac{8}{9}=\frac{(9\times3)+8}{9}=\frac{35}{9}$$
$$\frac{25}{6}\div\frac{35}{9}=\frac{25}{6} \times \frac{9}{35}= \frac{25\times9}{6\times35}$$
The HCF of 6 and 9 is 3.
The HCF of 35 and 25 is 5.
$$\frac{(25\div5)\times(9\div3)}{(35\div5)\times(6\div3)}=\frac{5\times3}{7\times2}=\frac{15}{14}=1\frac{1}{14}$$

record_links.rationale: This item asks learners to divide mixed numbers.

heading_path.h3: Exercise 6.9: Multiply and divide mixed numbers

record.evidence_quote: Source math retained: 6 rac{3}{10}= rac{(10 imes6)+3}{10}= rac{63}{10} 1 rac{4}{5}= rac{(5 imes1)+4}{5}= rac{9}{5} rac{63}{10}\div rac{9}{5}= rac{63}{10} \times \frac{5}{9}= \frac{63\times5}{10\times9} rac{(63\div9)\times(5\div5)}{(9\div9)\times(10\div5)}=\frac{7\times1}{1\times2}=\frac{7}{2}=3\frac{1}{2}
record.prompt_text:
### Exercise 6.9: Multiply and divide mixed numbers

5. $6\frac{3}{10}\div1\frac{4}{5}$
record.answer_text:
$$6\frac{3}{10}=\frac{(10\times6)+3}{10}=\frac{63}{10}$$
$$1\frac{4}{5}=\frac{(5\times1)+4}{5}=\frac{9}{5}$$
$$\frac{63}{10}\div\frac{9}{5}=\frac{63}{10} \times \frac{5}{9}= \frac{63\times5}{10\times9}$$
The HCF of 5 and 10 is 5.
The HCF of 63 and 9 is 9.
$$\frac{(63\div9)\times(5\div5)}{(9\div9)\times(10\div5)}=\frac{7\times1}{1\times2}=\frac{7}{2}=3\frac{1}{2}$$

record_links.rationale: This practical problem is solved by dividing a whole number by a fraction.

heading_path.h3: Exercise 6.10: Use operations with fractions to solve problems

record.evidence_quote: Source math retained: \frac{6}{15} \begin{array}{l}\phantom{00}50\div\frac{6}{15} \\ =50\times\frac{15}{6} \\ =\frac{50\times15}{6} \\ =\frac{750}{6} \\ = 125\end{array}
record.prompt_text:
### Exercise 6.10: Use operations with fractions to solve problems

6. A local store owner buys rice in bags of 50 kg. He then makes up smaller bags to sell. If a small bag is $\frac{6}{15}$ kg, how many small bags can he make up from one large bag?
record.answer_text:
$$\begin{array}{l}\phantom{00}50\div\frac{6}{15} \\newline =50\times\frac{15}{6} \\newline =\frac{50\times15}{6} \\newline =\frac{750}{6} \\newline =\;125\end{array}$$
The store owner can make up 125 small bags from one large bag.

record_links.rationale: This practical problem is solved by dividing one fraction by another fraction.

heading_path.h3: Exercise 6.10: Use operations with fractions to solve problems

record.evidence_quote: Source math retained: \frac{14}{16} \frac{1}{4} \frac{14}{16}\div\frac{1}{4}=\frac{14}{16}\times\frac{4}{1}=\frac{14\times4}{16\times1}=\frac{56}{16}=\frac{7}{2} =3\frac{1}{2} 3\frac{1}{2}
record.prompt_text:
### Exercise 6.10: Use operations with fractions to solve problems

7. There is $\frac{14}{16}$ litre of vegetable oil left in a bottle. A baker must measure this out in cups of $\frac{1}{4}$ litre each. How many cups will she measure out?
record.answer_text:
$$\frac{14}{16}\div\frac{1}{4}=\frac{14}{16}\times\frac{4}{1}=\frac{14\times4}{16\times1}=\frac{56}{16}=\frac{7}{2}=3\frac{1}{2}$$
The baker can measure out $3\frac{1}{2}$ cups.

record_links.rationale: This practical problem is solved by dividing mixed numbers.

heading_path.h3: Exercise 6.10: Use operations with fractions to solve problems

record.evidence_quote: Source math retained: 10\frac{5}{6} 2\frac{1}{2} 10\frac{5}{6}=\frac{65}{6} 2\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{2} \frac{65}{6}\div\frac{5}{2}=\frac{65}{6} \times \frac{2}{5}= \frac{65\times2}{6\times5} \frac{(65\div5)\times(2\div2)}{(5\div5)\times(6\div2)}=\frac{13\times1}{1\times3}=\frac{13}{3}=4\frac{1}{3} 4\frac{1}{3}
record.prompt_text:
### Exercise 6.10: Use operations with fractions to solve problems

10. A bag of garri has a mass of $10\frac{5}{6}$ kg. How many small packets, each with a mass of $2\frac{1}{2}$ kg, can be made up from the bag?
record.answer_text:
$$10\frac{5}{6}=\frac{65}{6}$$
$$2\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{2}$$
$$\frac{65}{6}\div\frac{5}{2}=\frac{65}{6} \times \frac{2}{5}= \frac{65\times2}{6\times5}$$
$$\frac{(65\div5)\times(2\div2)}{(5\div5)\times(6\div2)}=\frac{13\times1}{1\times3}=\frac{13}{3}=4\frac{1}{3}$$
$4\frac{1}{3}$ small packets can be made up.
